textureLab.title: Texture Laboratory
textureLab.description: Build and edit game-ready materials inside Blender, with procedural layers and a live texture-space workflow.

images.caption: A seamless clover ground texture made with TexLab on a material sphere
Viewport view of clover texture, viewing top-down normal in 2D space
This clover texture, rendered and combined with other TexLab ground textures in Unreal engine, blended in a landscape material

sections.title: Why this tool exists
sections.text: I wanted a material workflow that kept the parts I liked from dedicated texturing software while letting me work directly in Blender. Texture Laboratory grew from that need.

sections.title: A live texture-space workspace
sections.text: A geometry node system represents the model’s UV layout in a separate scene and follows changes to the source mesh. I can work in that space while switching between the individual maps and a lit preview.

sections.title: Editing the surface
sections.text: The system combines procedural materials, image inputs, and top-down geometry for normal-map detail and cleanup. It produces familiar maps such as base color, normal, roughness, metallic, emission, and opacity.

sections.title: Making the workflow reusable
sections.text: A shared material setup keeps the map outputs connected while leaving room for more complex materials. The gallery shows the authoring setup, material studies, and examples used in Unreal.

textureLab.label: Blender · Materials

openvat.title: OpenVAT
openvat.description: A Blender encoder and Unity playback system for bringing vertex animation into real-time projects.

images.caption: A modifier-driven deformation, baked with OpenVAT in Blender and played back in Unity.

sections.title: Why I made it
sections.text: I wanted an understandable, open-source route from Blender’s procedural deformation to a game engine. OpenVAT captures the motion in textures, then a shader uses that data to move the mesh on the GPU.

sections.title: My work
sections.text: I built the Blender tool and the Unity and Unreal integrations. Geometry Nodes drives the baking itself; Python handles the interface and the surrounding workflow. Working on the engine side let me explore how each renderer exposes its vertex stage, and where precision, normals, and import settings get in the way.

sections.title: Release and community
sections.text: OpenVAT is free and open source, with walkthroughs and engine examples on its own site. AntzGames also built a separate Godot integration. The links below cover the current tool, documentation, and source.

storyFeatures.title: Shared project data
paragraphs: I can define something once, use it across a game, and choose what can vary. Shared changes reach every use, while the editor keeps those relationships visible.
Libraries and bundles carry work between projects. Integrated Git lets me keep its history on my own SSDs and NAS.
storyFeatures.imageAlt: Close-up of a shared mesh, material, and script in PlushEngine’s data graph

storyFeatures.title: MCP tools
paragraphs: I built the editor’s MCP server and tools so assistants can inspect a project, look up the API, and help with authoring or scripts. They work through an interface I define inside the editor.
The point is less friction. I make the creative decisions.
storyFeatures.imageAlt: C# gameplay code open in PlushEngine’s Code tab
storyFeatures.caption: C# gameplay in the built-in Code tab.
storyFeatures.detailLabel: How I’ve bounded the MCP tools
detailParagraphs: I’m interested in shaping how assistants fit into creative tools, so I built the editor’s MCP server and the tools it exposes. MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets an assistant work with software through a defined interface. Building that connection myself means I can decide what useful assistance looks like inside the engine.

The tools work with the open game project: inspecting the scene, looking up the API, making authoring edits through plupy, and reading or changing project scripts. The assistant works through the editor’s APIs rather than clicking around the interface.

The integrated Codex and Claude Code connections use this same interface, with their usual shell, web, and file tools disabled. Authoring edits use the editor’s Undo system; C# script edits are compiled and have recovery copies. Those boundaries are part of the tool design.

I want help with repetitive setup, finding the right API, and understanding the systems I’m working with. I’m not building this to have an assistant generate games for me. The point is to reduce friction so I can spend more time making them, with the creative decisions staying with me.

storyFeatures.title: Music in the same project
paragraphs: I’ve made music with trackers for years. Building one into PlushEngine brings patterns, instruments, and effects alongside the game. It’s something I’ve always wanted in an editor.
storyFeatures.imageAlt: A close-up of pattern notes in the integrated music tracker
storyFeatures.caption: Notes from Laser Planet’s lobby sequence.

plush.technicalNotes: PlushEngine uses C# and .NET 10, an Avalonia editor, a Vulkan renderer through Silk.NET, and Slang shaders. Jolt and Box2D provide physics. Python supports authoring and automation; exported games use a separate runtime without the editor or Python. Mac and Windows exports are available in the engine; Linux and browser targets are experimental.
storyIntro: I've spent most of my career making tools that help other people make things. I'm a technical artist, which means I've spent an unreasonable amount of time learning how 3D software, game engines, animation systems, shaders, and all the other stuff underneath a game actually work (often just to find ways around limitations that probably shouldn't have existed in the first place).
Plush started because I wanted to own more of that process.

There are already some incredible game engines out there. I'm not making Plush because I think Unity, Unreal, or Godot are bad (although I certainly have opinions about some of their decisions). I just wanted to build an environment where the underlying systems made sense to me, where I could change things when I wanted to, and where I wasn't constantly working around decisions somebody else had made about how I should be making games.
I also wanted to see if I could actually do it.

storyNotes.title: Making things
paragraphs: I've spent my career making tools that remove friction from creative work. The goal has always been to make artists and developers more efficient, so they can spend less time fighting software and more time actually making something. But there's a distinction between eliminating unnecessary parts of a process and eliminating the process entirely.

If a five-year-old can ask a computer to make a game about trucks, and it just makes the game, that's pretty incredible. I'm not opposed to that existing. But personally, I don't particularly want a computer to make a game for me. I want to make the game. I want to understand how it works, mess around with the systems, break something, figure out why it broke, and occasionally discover something I hadn't even considered when I started.
And I think there's value in preserving that experience, even if the technology eventually makes it unnecessary.

storyNotes.title: Ownership
paragraphs: I don't particularly like that so much of the software we use has become something we rent. Subscriptions, mandatory accounts, online authentication, services that can disappear, updates that change things whether you want them to or not. You can spend years creating something with a tool and still depend on the company that made the tool to continue granting you access to it.
I think there's something important about that kind of ownership that we've gradually lost with digital software.

That doesn't mean I think every program needs to be open source, or that buying something should entitle you to every future version of it. Developers need to make money, and intellectual property rights exist for good reasons. But I do think that when you buy a piece of software, you should be able to keep using the version you bought without needing continued permission from whoever sold it to you.
I want Plush to work that way.

And perhaps more importantly, I want to be able to use Plush without depending on AI, or Adobe, or Epic, or whoever else might decide to change the terms of something I rely on. I want to open the editor, write some ordinary C#, use Python to automate whatever I need, import my own models and animations, and make games. If I want an AI agent to help me do something, great. But I don't want the agent to become a requirement for understanding or operating my own software.

storyNotes.title: Using AI
paragraphs: I've been using AI to help me program for years, long before agents could directly modify entire codebases. Initially that meant asking ChatGPT questions about APIs, getting code snippets, figuring out how to structure projects, and generally using it as a much more interactive version of Stack Overflow. I learned a tremendous amount of Python and C# that way (my formal programming education was primarily C++, and I don't think making tic-tac-toe for a college final particularly prepared me to write a game engine).

Now AI can implement entire systems, and I've used that extensively while developing Plush. I'm not going to pretend I wrote every line myself, because I didn't. But I also don't particularly like the idea of calling it a collaborative effort between myself and an AI. I wouldn't say Visual Studio co-authored my software, or that a shader I wrote was co-authored by the person whose research paper I referenced. AI is an incredibly powerful tool, and it's changed what I'm capable of accomplishing, but the decisions about what I'm building and why I'm building it are mine.
There's a certain irony in using AI to build a game engine partly because I don't want to depend on AI to make games. I'm aware of that (and I think it's a pretty interesting distinction).

sections.title: The problem
sections.text: Blender already has capable texture baking, but repeatedly selecting objects, preparing scenes, and organizing outputs made the process slower and more fragile than I wanted.

sections.title: What I built
sections.text: xBake puts source and target selection, batches of map types, and export formatting into one interface. It takes the parts of my baking workflow I used most and makes them easier to repeat.

sections.title: A more deliberate workflow
sections.text: Source and target objects can be assigned directly, with a single-object mode for simpler jobs. Outputs use configurable names and destinations, and the tool cleans up after the bake to keep the working file manageable.

sections.title: The technical work
sections.text: The tool handles a range of bake types and map conventions, including 16-bit output where appropriate, raw color space, and normalization. It combines interface design with the details that make maps usable in a game art pipeline.

xbake.label: Blender · Texture baking
xbake.description: A texture baking workflow built around explicit source objects, consistent outputs, and less setup.

aether.title: Aether
aether.description: My geometry-first material authoring system for Blender: editable surface construction in, coherent texture sets and game-ready props out.

images.caption: Earlier xBake output: geometry, the baked normal map, and the textured model.
TextureLab material creation and texture-space workflow.
A clover ground material created with TextureLab.
TextureLab ground materials blended in an Unreal landscape.

sections.title: What it is
sections.text: Aether is the current home for xBake and TextureLab. I’m bringing texture baking and material creation into one Blender tool, so preparing a model, working on its surface, and exporting the maps can happen in the same workflow.

sections.title: The material tools
sections.text: The TextureLab side uses a live texture-space workspace built with Geometry Nodes. It combines procedural materials, image inputs, and geometry-based detail, with previews of the individual maps and the finished surface.

sections.title: The baking tools
sections.text: The xBake side handles source and target objects, batches of maps, naming, and output settings. Aether adds the scene setup and material-building work around that process, including source-map baking and material conversion.

sections.title: Current work and earlier images
sections.text: I’m actively developing Aether. The videos and images here are from xBake and TextureLab, the tools it grew from; they show the material work and workflow ideas rather than the latest interface.

sections.title: What I’m working on
sections.text: Sprite Toolkit is the current home for my Blender 2D tools, previously shown here as Pixels and 2D Tools. I’m continuing the work on image and layer editing, pixel alignment, and getting useful 2D output from a Blender scene.

sections.title: The workflow
sections.text: The earlier tools manage image planes, pivots, orthographic cameras, and the relationship between scene units and output pixels. The current code expands that work with layers, masks, effects, compositions, and export tools.
